comments.body:
I don't know why `labels` is ignored, nor do I immediately see a reason why it couldn't be supported.  It looks like this was done during the initial `IntervalIndex` implementation, which was before my time, so I'm not entirely sure what the historical context is for this.  If I had to venture a guess, I'd say it's not so much that this can't be supported, but more so that it'd take a bit work to do properly.

The `_bins_to_cuts` function is what's responsible for applying the `labels`, and it currently has an `IntervalIndex` fastpath that ignores `labels`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/453fa85a8b88ca22c7b878a3fcf97e068f11b6c4/pandas/core/reshape/tile.py#L327-L332

I'm not sure what the optimal way for implementing `labels` with an `IntervalIndex` is, but I see two general approaches.  The first would be to just add on `labels` specific code to the `IntervalIndex` fastpath.  This could be viable if implementation is either short or significantly different enough from the existing code, but my worry is that this could lead to duplicate code that would become a burden to maintain.

The other approach would be to refactor `_bins_to_cuts` in a more generic way to handle both without impacting performance.  There could be some minor annoyances here to reconcile, e.g. the first thing that comes to mind is that for `IntervalIndex` you want `labels` to be the same length as `bins`, but when `bins` is an array you want `bins` to have one extra element (`n + 1` endpoints --> `n` intervals), and I suspect there'd be other similar things.

I don't think either approach would be particularly difficult, but would just require a bit of work to make sure that existing functionality is unchanged, and that it's implemented in a maintainable way.

issues.title: BUG: Collection of inconsistencies in .astype conversions
issues.body:
I have a use case where (automatic) casting between the following `pandas` dtypes is necessary;

`bool`, `boolean`, `int64`, `Int64`, `float64`, `object` and `string`.

Note that `boolean`, `Int64` and `string` are the new pandas 1.0 nullable dtypes.

The default approach for this would be `series.astype(target_dtype)`, for `target_dtype` one of the above dtypes as strings. This works (given no issues with missings) but for the inconsistencies below:

```python
In [1]: import pandas as pd
   ...: import numpy as np
```

#### `pd.NA` to `float`:
Summary: Casting `float(pd.NA)` raises a `TypeError` (as does casting `float(None)`). While `np.array([None, "1"]).astype("float")` works (and gets called [here](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/31db14c489224e92fcc8729ad44a2ebb5114db22/pandas/core/dtypes/cast.py#L1122)), the same call with `pd.NA` fails.
```python
In [2]: pd.Series(["1", "2", pd.NA], dtype="object").astype("float")
TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a number, not 'NAType'

In [3]: pd.Series(["1", "2", pd.NA], dtype="string").astype("float")
TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a number, not 'NAType'

In [4]: pd.Series(["1", "2", pd.NA], dtype="string").astype("category").astype("float")  # magic workaround
Out[4]: 
0    1.0
1    2.0
2    NaN
dtype: float64
```
Edit: Fixed with https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/37974.

#### `object` / `string` to `Int64` (nullable)
Summary: `object` columns cannot be casted to `Int64`. Casting 
- `object` -> `string` -> `Int64` works.
- `object` -> `float` -> `Int64` works if the data does not contain `pd.NA` (see above)
- `object` -> `int64` -> `Int64` works if the data does not contain missings.

```python
In [5]: pd.Series(["1", "2", "3"]).astype("Int64")
TypeError: object cannot be converted to an IntegerDtype

In [5]: pd.Series(["1", "2", "3"], dtype="string").astype("Int64")
Out[5]: 
0    1
1    2
2    3
dtype: Int64

In [6]:  pd.Series(["1", "2", "3"]).astype("int").astype("Int64")
Out[6]:
0    1
1    2
2    3
dtype: Int64

In [7]:  pd.Series(["1", "2", None]).astype("int").astype("Int64")  # int columns cannot contain missings
TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a number, not 'NoneType'

In [8]:  pd.Series(["1", "2", None]).astype("float").astype("Int64")  # magic workaround
Out[8]:
0       1
1       2
2    <NA>
dtype: Int64

In [9]: pd.Series(["1", "2", pd.NA], dtype="object").astype("float").astype("Int64")  # see pd.NA -> float
TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a number, not 'NAType'

In [10]: pd.Series(["1", "2", pd.NA], dtype="object").astype("string").astype("Int64")
Out[10]: 
0       1
1       2
2    <NA>
dtype: Int64
```
Related: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/25472#issuecomment-630752912

#### `string` / `object` to `bool` or `boolean`
Summary: Casting `string` or `object` columns to `bool` or `boolean` behaves strangely. I am not sure what the expected behaviour for `string` / `object` to `bool` / `boolean` should be. It would be nice to have consistent behaviour.
- `string` / `object` -> `bool` works if there are no missings, but yields only `True`
- `string` / `object` -> `boolean` raises

```python
In [11]: pd.Series(["True", "False", "bogus"], dtype="string").astype("bool")  # everything is True
Out[11]:
0    True
1    True
2    True
dtype: bool

In [12]: pd.Series(["True", "False", "bogus"], dtype="object").astype("bool")
Out[12]:
0    True
1    True
2    True
dtype: bool

In [13]: pd.Series(["True", "False", "bogus"], dtype="string").astype("boolean")
TypeError: data type not understood

In [14]: pd.Series(["True", "False", "bogus"], dtype="object").astype("boolean")
TypeError: Need to pass bool-like values
```

#### `int` (non-nullable) to `boolean`
Summary: Casting from (non-nullable) `int64` to (nullable) `boolean` raises.
 - `int64` -> `Int64` -> `boolean` works
 - `int64` -> `bool` -> `boolean` works as long as there are no missings.

comments.body:
I can confirm this reproduces on both pandas 2.3.3 and the current main branch. The failure happens in pandas/core/indexes/base.py, inside Index.set_names (around line 2125) and Index._set_names (lines 1993-1996).

set_names only wraps names in a single-element list when is_list_like(names) is False (line 2125: "if not is_list_like(names): names = [names]"). Tuples are list-like, so a tuple passed as names is forwarded to _set_names unchanged. _set_names then requires len(values) == 1 for a non-MultiIndex (line 1996: "raise ValueError(f'Length of new names must be 1, got {len(values)}')"), which is why a 3-tuple raises here even though the index has only one level.

Index construction does not go through this path at all. The name argument passed to Index(...) is stored directly as a single hashable value, with no is_list_like branching, so a tuple of any length is accepted there without being interpreted as a sequence of per-level names.

Two data points make the inconsistency easier to see. A length-1 tuple works fine through rename_axis/set_names, because it happens to satisfy len(values) == 1, which masks the issue for that specific case. A 3-tuple also works fine through set_names/rename_axis when the index actually is a 3-level MultiIndex, because there it is correctly interpreted as three separate level names. So the failure is specific to using a tuple whose length differs from 1 as the name for a non-Multi Index.

This looks like a genuine inconsistency rather than intentional design. The same tuple value is accepted as an atomic name at construction time but rejected, or silently reinterpreted, at rename time purely because of the is_list_like check treating tuples as name sequences. A fix would need set_names/_set_names to distinguish between a tuple used as one hashable name and a sequence of per-level names, which is inherently ambiguous given how MultiIndex also uses tuples internally. Worth deciding intentionally before the stubs are updated, since whichever behavior is chosen will need to be typed accordingly.

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(data={"A": ["1", "NaN"]})
```

had a look at where this comes from . reproduces on 3.0.5 .

the flag that decides whether coerce gives a real null is in `pandas/core/tools/numeric.py` :

```python
convert_to_masked_nullable=dtype_backend is not lib.no_default
or (
    isinstance(values_dtype, StringDtype)
    and values_dtype.na_value is libmissing.NA
),
```

`string[pyarrow]` is an `ArrowDtype` , not a `StringDtype` , so neither side is true , no mask comes back and the parse failure ends up as a plain float nan . that is why it works for `StringDtype` , it is named there and arrow is not .

**but adding arrow to that condition is not enough , and on its own it makes things worse .** with just that one line changed :

```python
pd.to_numeric(pd.Series(["1", None, "x"]).convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow"), errors="coerce")

# on 3.0.5 as it is :  [1.0, <NA>, nan]      the null survives , the bad value is a float nan
# with the one line  :  [1,   <NA>, 1]       the bad value became 1
```

it invents a value . the reason is the two masks are never put together . for an arrow input the code does

```python
mask = values.isna()                  # full length
values = values.dropna().to_numpy()   # shorter
```

then `maybe_convert_numeric` returns a `new_mask` sized to the shorter array , and `values = values[~new_mask]` shrinks it again . i printed the shapes on that example :

```
mask=(3,)  new_mask=(2,)  values=(1,)
```

the merge below only takes `new_mask` when the shapes match , which they cannot when any null was dropped , so `mask` stays the original null mask and `data[~mask] = values` has one value for two open slots . numpy broadcasts it into both .

so the fix needs the original null mask and the parse failure mask combined against the original positions , not just the flag flipped .

i have not sent a patch . pandas needs a cython build here and i have not run your suite , so i only know the behaviour , not what else depends on it . happy to put one together with tests for both cases if you want it .

adding `ArrowDtype` to that condition on its own is not enough . it turns the nan into a real

with `["1", None, "x"]` and `errors="coerce"` you get `[1, <NA>, 1]` . the `1` on the end is

issues.title: BUG: `Series.str.extract` with `ArrowDtype` raises on unnamed capture groups, and drops them when mixed with named ones
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import re

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa

ser = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string()))

# 1. all groups named - works
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(?P<digit>\d)")

# 2. no group named - ValueError
ser.str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
# ValueError: pat='([ab])(\\d)' must contain a symbolic group name.

# 3. named and unnamed mixed - ArrowInvalid
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)")
# pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Regular expression contains unnamed groups

# 4. same mixed pattern, but with flags (main only) - silently wrong
ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)", flags=re.IGNORECASE)
#   letter     1
# 0      a  <NA>
# 1      b  <NA>

# every one of these works on object, str and StringDtype:
pd.Series(["a1", "b2"]).str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
pd.Series(["a1", "b2"], dtype="string[pyarrow]").str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
#    0  1
# 0  a  1
# 1  b  2
```

### Issue Description

`ArrowExtensionArray._str_extract` is the only `_str_extract` that requires capture groups to be
named, and `ArrowDtype` is the only dtype routed to it (`StringDtype`, `dtype="string[pyarrow]"`
included, resolves to `ObjectStringArrayMixin._str_extract` via `ArrowStringArray`'s MRO).
`pc.extract_regex` addresses its result struct by field name, so `_str_extract` builds the result
from `compiled.groupindex` alone. Three failures follow:

| pattern | behavior |
| --- | --- |
| all groups named | correct |
| no group named | `ValueError: ... must contain a symbolic group name.` - guard in `_str_extract` |
| named + unnamed mixed | `ArrowInvalid: Regular expression contains unnamed groups` - from the kernel; the guard misses it, `groupindex` being non-empty |
| named + unnamed mixed, with `flags` | **silent data loss**: the `re` fallback iterates `groupindex`, so the unnamed group comes back all-`<NA>` while `_get_group_names` still labels it. `main` only; 3.0.5 raises `NotImplementedError` for non-zero `flags`. |

The last row is the concerning one. A full-shaped DataFrame with a silently empty column.

The accessor rejects only patterns with *zero* capture groups, so one unnamed group is valid as
far as the public API goes - this is a backend-dependent restriction on a dtype-agnostic method,
and undocumented: the docstring's own example extracts an unnamed group into column `0`.

**Related**

- #56268 - reported case 2 (via `read_csv(dtype_backend="pyarrow")`), closed by #56334, the PR
  that implemented `str.extract` for `ArrowDtype`: named groups handled, `ValueError` for the
  rest. Its reproducer still fails verbatim on 3.0.5. Cases 3 and 4 were never reported.
- #53846 - adjacent, `extractall` dtype preservation rather than capture groups.

### Expected Behavior

`.str.extract` should behave identically across dtypes: unnamed groups labelled by position,
named groups by name, and the two mixable - matching `_get_group_names` in the accessor,
which already computes exactly those labels.

```python
ser.str.extract(r"([ab])(\d)")
#         0       1
# 0       a       1
# 1       b       2

ser.str.extract(r"(?P<letter>[ab])(\d)")
#   letter       1
# 0      a       1
# 1      b       2
```

This does not require new machinery. `_str_extract` already has an elementwise `re` fallback
for the cases `pc.extract_regex` cannot serve (`flags`, compiled `re.Pattern`). Routing any
pattern with an unnamed group through that same fallback, and labelling by position rather
than by `groupindex`, resolves all four cases above. Happy to open a PR.

```
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Darwin
```

issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

assert pd.__version__ == "3.0.5"
assert np.__version__ == "2.5.1"

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01 00:00:01"],  # <- value dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),
    strict=False
)

np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.001"],
    pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    ["1970-01-01T00:00:01.000"],  # <- unit dependent format
    pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),
    strict=False
)
```

### Issue Description

The string formatting of datetimes depends on the values rather than the time unit of the data type. The analogous operation in NumPy only depends on the unit.

I was not able to find a definitive answer on the matter that clarified whether this is intended behavior. I can see that this may have been intended in pandas 1.x where the one and only unit was `ns` which would lead to very long strings in all cases, despite most users probably never working on a ns resolution. 

### Expected Behavior

My understanding is that value-dependent semantics are not desired in pandas these days(?). Given that pandas allows users to define their desired units these days, it seems reasonable to me to make the formatting depend only on the unit rather than the values. 

Alternatively, it may be nice to document the intended formatting semantics (unless I missed them and that is already the case).

comments.body:
For the `datetime64[ms]` case in your example, an explicit format provides consistent output while keeping the Series index:

```python
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 1000, None], dtype="datetime64[ms]")

formatted = (
    s.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f")
    .str.slice(stop=-3)
)

assert formatted.iloc[0] == "1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"
assert formatted.iloc[1] == "1970-01-01 00:00:01.000"
assert pd.isna(formatted.iloc[2])
```

For these millisecond-resolution values, `%f` produces six fractional digits; removing the final three leaves a fixed three-digit millisecond field, including `.000`. Missing values remain missing.

This is specifically a millisecond-formatting workaround, not a general solution for preserving microsecond or nanosecond precision, and it does not settle whether `astype(str)` should change its behavior.

Reference: [`[Series.dt.strftime](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.dt.strftime.html)`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.dt.strftime.html).

issues.title: BUG: Series/DataFrame.replace with a callable value silently stores the function instead of applying or rejecting it
issues.body:
Passing a callable as `value` to `replace` stores the function object as the replacement data. It neither applies it nor raises:

```python
s = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"])
s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True)
# 0    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
# 1    <function <lambda> at 0x...>
```

Same for exact match without regex and for `DataFrame.replace`. Reproduced on 3.0.5.

`Series.str.replace` with the same arguments returns `["aX", "bX"]`, and the `replace` docs list `value` as scalar/dict/list/str/regex with no callables. GH#18634 set the precedent that invalid `replace` arguments raise, and the suite tests a callable `to_replace` raising, but nothing covers a callable `value`. On main (`pandas/core/generic.py`, `replace`), `to_replace` is validated up front and `value` is not checked at all.

The corruption spreads silently: the result is object dtype holding functions, `to_json` renders them as `{}`, and later string ops fail far from the mistake (`TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'function'`). Support callables or raise like `to_replace` does. Storing them should not happen.

issues.title: BUG: mixed int64/float64 Index operations falsely match distinct labels above 2**53
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

integer_label = 2**53 + 1                  # 9007199254740993
float_label = float(2**53)                 # 9007199254740992.0

integer_index = pd.Index([integer_label], dtype="int64")
float_index = pd.Index([float_label], dtype="float64")

print(integer_label == float_label)
print("equals:", integer_index.equals(float_index))

try:
    integer_index.get_loc(float_label)
except KeyError:
    print("get_loc: KeyError")

print("get_indexer:", integer_index.get_indexer(float_index))
print("intersection:", integer_index.intersection(float_index))
print("union:", integer_index.union(float_index))
print("difference:", integer_index.difference(float_index))

values = pd.Series(["payload"], index=integer_index)
print("reindex:")
print(values.reindex(float_index))

left = pd.Series([1], index=integer_index)
right = pd.Series([2], index=float_index)
print("aligned addition:")
print(left + right)


Output on pandas 3.0.5:


False
equals: True
get_loc: KeyError
get_indexer: [0]
intersection: Index([9007199254740993], dtype='int64')
union: Index([9007199254740992.0], dtype='float64')
difference: Index([], dtype='int64')
reindex:
9.007199e+15    payload
dtype: str
aligned addition:
9007199254740993    3
dtype: int64
```

### Issue Description

The two labels are distinct: Python equality returns `False`, and scalar `Index.get_loc` raises `KeyError`. However, `get_indexer` returns `[0]`. False matches also occur in Index set operations, reindexing, and arithmetic alignment.

This is not a case where the original integer has already been lost inside a float. The float label is exactly `2**53`, while the integer label is exactly `2**53 + 1`. They become equal only after the integer Index is cast to `float64` during mixed-dtype reconciliation.

Source inspection identifies more than one relevant path. For mismatched `int64`/`float64` dtypes, `get_indexer` calls `_find_common_type_compat`, casts both operands to `float64`, and then calls `_get_indexer`. This conversion rounds `2**53 + 1` to `2**53`.

Separately, `Index.equals` compares the underlying arrays through `array_equivalent` and returns `True` for these two Index objects. Both `intersection` and `difference` have early-return paths based on `Index.equals`, before their general matching logic. The observed results should therefore not all be attributed solely to `get_indexer`.

The practical consequence is silent association of data with a different label. Large numeric identifiers, transaction numbers, or similar keys can reach this path when one source uses `int64` and another uses `float64`, for example after an import or missing-value-driven conversion.

Related but distinct: #61676 and #66794 concern false matches in `isin`. That path now returns `False` for this pair on current main, while `get_indexer`, set operations, reindexing, and alignment still produce the results above. Merge dtype/precision reports such as #8596 and #61688 concern different APIs.

I found no identical public Issue or PR in searches for the concrete value `9007199254740993`, `2**53`, mixed `int64`/`float64` Index operations, and `get_indexer`. This does not guarantee that no duplicate exists.

### Automated tools disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text before submission.

### Expected Behavior

Mixed numeric Index operations should not match labels that are unequal before dtype reconciliation. For the example above:

```text
integer_index.get_indexer(float_index) -> array([-1])
integer_index.intersection(float_index) -> empty Index
integer_index.union(float_index) -> two distinct labels
integer_index.difference(float_index) -> the original integer label
values.reindex(float_index) -> missing value, not "payload"
left + right -> two distinct labels with missing values
```

The exact result dtype for operations that must contain both labels may require a compatibility decision, but both exact values must be preserved as distinct labels.

To help catalogue the relevant APIs, I compared how they handle the following two distinct values. Each Index contains one key.

```python
import pandas as pd

integer_key = 9007199254740993      # 2**53 + 1
```

| API / operation | Float key against an integer Index | Integer key against a float Index |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get_loc` / `key in index` | No match | Match |
| `.loc[scalar_key]` | `KeyError` | Returns the value |
| `Index.equals` | `True` | `True` |
| `get_indexer` / `.loc[key_array]` | Match | Match |
| `Series.map` with a Series or dictionary | Returns the mapped value | Returns the mapped value |
| `Series.map(mapping.get)` | No match | No match |
| `reindex` / assigning a Series to a DataFrame column | Carries over the value | Carries over the value |
| `intersection` | Retains the integer key | Retains the float key |
| `union` / `difference` | One float key / empty | One float key / empty |
| Inner `merge` using indexes or columns | Joins the rows | Joins the rows |

In particular, the comparison shows differences in:

- **Lookup form:** scalar keys versus arrays of keys.
- **Mapper form:** passing a dictionary to `map` versus passing its `get` method.
- **Scalar lookup direction:** a float key against an integer Index versus an integer key against a float Index.

still there on 3.0.5 .

```
is_list_like(MyEnum)   = False
DataFrame(columns=MyEnum) -> TypeError: Index(...) must be called with a collection of some kind
```

the cause is one line in `c_is_list_like` in `pandas/_libs/lib.pyx` :

```python
getattr(obj, "__iter__", None) is not None and not isinstance(obj, type)
```

`not isinstance(obj, type)` throws out every class . it is there so `list` itself does not count as list like , which is right . but an enum class really is iterable , because `EnumMeta` puts `__iter__` on the metaclass , so this rules out something that does iterate .

python looks special methods up on the type , not on the object , so `getattr(type(obj), "__iter__", None)` tells the two apart on its own and the class exclusion is not needed :

```
object                 iter() works   type has __iter__
MyEnum (the class)     yes            True
list (the class)       no             False
dict (the class)       no             False
str (the class)        no             False
[1,2,3]                yes            True
'abc'                  yes            True
5                      no             False
```

it agrees with `iter()` on every one of those , which the current check does not . strings and generic aliases are excluded on the lines below anyway so they are not affected .

one thing i have not done . pandas needs a cython build and i have not run your test suite , so i do not know what else leans on the current behaviour . anything whose instance carries `__iter__` as a plain attribute rather than on its class would stop being list like , which is closer to what python does but is still a change . happy to send a patch with tests if you want it .

issues.title: BUG: `.loc[:, [*labels]]` inconsistently reorders `MultiIndex`ed `Series` and `DataFrame`s
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> sorted_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("cdef")])
>>> unsorted_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("fdec")])
>>> sorted_labels = ["d", "e"]
>>> unsorted_labels = ["e", "d"]
>>> sorted_s = pd.Series(range(len(sorted_index)), sorted_index)
>>> sorted_s
a  c    0
   d    1
   e    2
   f    3
b  c    4
   d    5
   e    6
   f    7
dtype: int64
>>> sorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]
a  d    1
   e    2
b  d    5
   e    6
dtype: int64
>>> sorted_s.loc[:, unsorted_labels]
a  e    2
b  e    6
a  d    1
b  d    5
dtype: int64
>>> unsorted_s = pd.Series(range(len(unsorted_index)), unsorted_index)
>>> unsorted_s
a  f    0
   d    1
   e    2
   c    3
b  f    4
   d    5
   e    6
   c    7
dtype: int64
>>> unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]
a  d    1
b  d    5
a  e    2
b  e    6
dtype: int64
>>> unsorted_s.loc[:, unsorted_labels]
a  e    2
b  e    6
a  d    1
b  d    5
dtype: int64
```

### Issue Description

When indexing a `MultiIndex`ed `DataFrame` or `Series` via `.loc[:, [*labels]]`, the second level "takes precedence" (for lack of a better term) over the first level if the second level of the `MultiIndex` is unsorted *or* if the `labels` are unsorted. This could be considered unexpected behavior because it means the order of the result depends on the order in which unselected labels appear in the index as well as `_lexsort_depth`. This issue may be related to #31330 and #40978.

The dependency on `_lexsort_depth` is particularly troubling to me for several reasons. First, it means that the order of the result depends not only on whether the list-indexed level is sorted, but also whether all previous levels are sorted. In the following example, `looks_sorted_s` looks identical to `sorted_index`, but the codes of the two labels in the first level are swapped, making it technically unsorted:
```python
>>> looks_sorted_index = pd.MultiIndex(
...     [list("ba"), list("cdef")], [[1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3]]
... )
>>> looks_sorted_s = pd.Series(range(len(looks_sorted_index)), looks_sorted_index)
>>> looks_sorted_s
a  c    0
   d    1
   e    2
   f    3
b  c    4
   d    5
   e    6
   f    7
dtype: int64
>>> looks_sorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]
a  d    1
b  d    5
a  e    2
b  e    6
dtype: int64
```
The converse is also true:
```python
>>> looks_unsorted_index = pd.MultiIndex(
...     [list("ab"), list("fdec")], [[0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3]]
... )
>>> looks_unsorted_s = pd.Series(range(len(looks_unsorted_index)), looks_unsorted_index)
>>> looks_unsorted_s
a  f    0
   d    1
   e    2
   c    3
b  f    4
   d    5
   e    6
   c    7
dtype: int64
>>> looks_unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]
a  d    1
   e    2
b  d    5
   e    6
dtype: int64
```
...which brings me to how I discovered the issue. [The documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html) suggests to me that the *labels*, rather than the codes, must be lexicographically sorted in all levels up to `sortlevel`. Functions like `pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays` impose this requirement:
```python
>>> pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("fdec")], sortorder=2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "~/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pandas/core/indexes/multi.py", line 686, in from_product
    return cls(levels, codes, sortorder=sortorder, names=names)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "~/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pandas/core/indexes/multi.py", line 365, in __new__
    new_codes = result._verify_integrity()
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "~/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pandas/core/indexes/multi.py", line 459, in _verify_integrity
    raise ValueError(
ValueError: Value for sortorder must be inferior or equal to actual lexsort_depth: sortorder 2 with lexsort_depth 1
```
...but various other functions do not:
```python
>>> idx = pd.IndexSlice
>>> unsorted_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("dc")])
>>> unsorted_df = pd.DataFrame({"f": range(4), "e": range(4, 8)}, unsorted_index)
>>> unsorted_df
     f  e
a d  0  4
  c  1  5
b d  2  6
  c  3  7
>>> unsorted_df.index._lexsort_depth
1
>>> unsorted_df.loc[idx[:, ["d", "c"]],]
     f  e
a d  0  4
b d  2  6
a c  1  5
b c  3  7
>>> sorted_df = unsorted_df.stack(future_stack=True).unstack(0)
>>> sorted_df
     a  b
c f  1  3
  e  5  7
d f  0  2
  e  4  6
>>> sorted_df.index._lexsort_depth
2
>>> sorted_df.loc[idx[:, ["f", "e"]],]
     a  b
c f  1  3
  e  5  7
d f  0  2
  e  4  6
```
Note: I'm not sure if this is an issue yet, but while `stack` (regardless of the value of `future_stack`) uses the same codes as `self`, `unstack` does not. Furthermore, `unstack` uses the order of first appearance rather than lexicographic order. I will dig into this later this week.

While the docs consistently use the phrase "Level of sortedness (must be lexicographically sorted by that level)", they freely exchange the idea of lexicographically sorted labels/"levels" (*e.g.*, [`MultiIndex.from_arrays`](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.from_arrays.html#pandas.MultiIndex.from_arrays)) with lexicographically sorted codes (*e.g.*, [`MultiIndex`](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.MultiIndex.html#pandas.MultiIndex)). It also doesn't help that functions like `unstack` map labels to codes by order of appearance rather than lexicographical order, but again, it's not yet clear to me how `unstack` remaps labels (or if it even should). I still need to go through the implementation of `unstack` and a few others like `MultiIndex.remove_unused_levels` for comparison.

> For indexing, it does seem beneficial to me to keep the result sorted when possible. It seems to me we can interpret `sorted_s.loc[:, unsorted_labels]` as a request for the 2nd level in the order of `unsorted_labels` only after maintain the order of prior levels. However I would weigh heavily here the performance implications as well as the code churn. I think further investigations would be welcome, but it could be a high bar for making a change here.

I am of the opinion that indexing with a label list should not behave any differently than indexing with an equivalent boolean array (when an equivalent boolean array exists), and this is currently not the case with `unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]`. Perhaps I am alone here, but I most often use

* `unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]` as a shorthand for `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.get_level_values(0), sorted_labels]`
* `unsorted_s.loc[:, labels1, labels2]` as a shorthand for `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.isin(labels1, 1) & unsorted_s.index.isin(labels2, 2)]` or `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.droplevel().isin(pd.MultiIndex.from_product([labels1, labels2]))]`
* *etc.*

(As an aside, it seems rather odd to me that `MultiIndex.isin` cannot operate on a selection of levels.)

and I would expect a lot of people who also work with a lot of raw NumPy arrays would expect it to function as such. But besides that, the real pain point for me is that it does so *inconsistently* depending on invisible factors like which function mapped the labels to codes. If you don't want to rely on private members like `_lexsort_depth`, you have to jump through a lot of hoops to programmatically determine how the result will be ordered. If the performance implications/code churn mean the expected behavior should instead be such that label lists *always* take precedence over slices, then so be it:
```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> sorted_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("cdef")])
>>> unsorted_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([list("ab"), list("fdec")])
>>> sorted_labels = ["d", "e"]
>>> unsorted_labels = ["e", "d"]
>>> sorted_s = pd.Series(range(len(sorted_index)), sorted_index)
>>> sorted_s
a  c    0
   d    1
   e    2
   f    3
b  c    4
   d    5
   e    6
   f    7
dtype: int64
>>> sorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]
a  d    1

b  e    2

>>> ...
```

issues.title: BUG: tz-aware Timestamp with a year outside 1-9999 is stored as year 1970 or 1972 in Series/DatetimeIndex
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Year 10000 fits easily in datetime64[us]; the scalar is correct.
ts = pd.Timestamp(np.datetime64("10000-03-05T12:00", "us")).tz_localize("UTC")
print(ts.year)                                    # 10000

print(pd.Series([ts])[0].year)                    # 1972  (expected 10000)
print(pd.DatetimeIndex([ts])[0].year)             # 1972
print(pd.to_datetime([ts])[0].year)               # 1972

# A non-leap year becomes 1970 instead.
ts2 = pd.Timestamp(np.datetime64("10001-03-05T12:00", "us")).tz_localize("UTC")
print(pd.Series([ts2])[0].year)                   # 1970  (expected 10001)

# Without a time zone the same value is stored correctly.
print(pd.Series([ts.tz_localize(None)])[0].year)  # 10000
```

### Issue Description

A tz-aware `Timestamp` that year is outside Python `datetime` range (1-9999) is valid with a non-nanosecond unit and the scalar behaves correctly. However when it is converted into datetime64 storage (`Series`, `DataFrame`, `Index`, `DatetimeIndex`, `pd.array`, `to_datetime`, or `.astype("datetime64[us, UTC]")` from object), the stored year silently becomes **1972** for a leap year or **1970** otherwise. Month, day and time are correct. There is no warning and no error. Years below 1 are affected the same way: year 0 becomes 1972 and year -1 becomes 1970.

Tz-naive values are not affected and the scalar operations also (`tz_convert`, `Timestamp(ts)`).

**Likely cause.** For out-of-range years, `create_timestamp_from_ts` (`tslibs/timestamps.pyx`) builds the underlying `datetime` with a placeholder year, 1972 or 1970, and keeps the real year in `_year`. Its comment warns that `PyDateTime_GET_YEAR` is therefore unreliable.

In `parse_pydatetime` (`tslibs/conversion.pyx`), naive `Timestamp`s use `_value` directly. Tz-aware values instead go through `convert_datetime_to_tsobject`, then `pydatetime_to_dtstruct` (`tslibs/np_datetime.pyx`). That function reads `dt.year` and says in a comment that this avoids `PyDateTime_GET_YEAR`. However, `dt` is typed `datetime`, and under Cython 3 `dt.year` compiles to the inline property in `cpython/datetime.pxd`, which is `PyDateTime_GET_YEAR`. So the placeholder year is stored.

This is the same mechanism as #53125, which was fixed in `offsets.pyx` by reading `(<_Timestamp>stamp)._year`.


### Expected Behavior

The stored value should be the same  as the scalar: year 10000 and 10001 in the example as it already is for tz-naive values. If those years are not to be supported for tz-aware data the `OutOfBoundsDatetime` should be raised. Silently changing the year should not happen.

I think that the another way to solve that I did not tested: in `parse_pydatetime`, handle a tz-aware `_Timestamp` the way the naive branch does, since its `_value` is already UTC. Or have `pydatetime_to_dtstruct` read the year through the Python attribute instead of the C macro.

Also reproduced on pandas 3.0.5 and on main (`3.2.0.dev0+371.gbb4297c4e6`, commit bb4297c4e6fc0fd8afc2d05c4bd4b51596d20264). Kernel version lines removed below.

issues.title: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6)
# TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'

df2 = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0, 5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")})
df2.loc[:, "A"] = df2["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # OK
```

### Issue Description

On a 1-row DataFrame, df.loc[:, col] = <NumPy ndarray/Series> into an existing PyArrow-backed column raises TypeError, even when every value is a valid float (e.g. 5000.0). The same assignment succeeds when the frame has 2 or more rows.

5000.0 is not invalid. The error text is misleading.

What happens:

The RHS is a length-1 float64 array, array([5000.]).
SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace unwraps any 1-d length-1 ndarray to a 0-d array to avoid the NumPy 1.25 deprecation (value[0, ...], added in [#52906](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/52906)):
if isinstance(value, np.ndarray) and value.ndim == 1 and len(value) == 1:
    value = value[0, ...]  # array([5000.]) -> array(5000.)
is_list_like(array(5000.)) is False, so ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa takes the scalar path.
pa.scalar(np.ndarray(...), type=pa.float64()) fails:
ArrowInvalid: Could not convert array(5000.) with type numpy.ndarray: tried to convert to double
pandas 3 rewraps that as TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]' and, unlike 2.x, does not fall back to recasting the column.
This is the same unwrap that #59249 / #57923 / #65452 discuss for object-dtype cells. Here the symptom is different and is a hard error on valid numeric data, not an API question about whether a cell should store array([1.]) vs 1.0.

Related, but not the same report:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/59249
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57923
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65452

### Expected Behavior

A valid float should be written into the double[pyarrow] column. 1-row and N-row frames should behave the same.

A narrow fix would be enough and does not require settling the whole single-element listlike-RHS matrix in #65452, for example:

in _box_pa_scalar, if value is a 0-d ndarray, use value.item() before pa.scalar, or
in setitem_inplace, skip the length-1 unwrap when the target is an ExtensionArray.

### Installed Versions

<details>

python   : 3.13.5
pandas   : 3.0.5   (also reproduced the failure mode on 3.0.6 source; main still has the unwrap)
pyarrow  : 25.0.0
numpy    : 2.5.2
OS       : Windows

On pandas 2.2.3 / 2.3.3 the same assignment does not raise. It emits

FutureWarning: Setting an item of incompatible dtype is deprecated...

and recasts the column to NumPy float64. pandas 3 turned that warning into this TypeError, so the 1-row unwrap now surfaces as a hard failure on Arrow columns.

Confirmed on all released pandas 3.0.x; 3.0.6 fixed a different loc[:, col] Arrow issue (GH 67990, CoW aliasing), not this one.

</details>

issues.title: BUG: cumsum/cumprod raises ArrowInvalid: overflow on integer ArrowDtypes instead of upcasting
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

s = pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]")

s.cumsum()                                    # ArrowInvalid: overflow
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8").cumsum()  # [100, 200], dtype int64
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="Int8").cumsum()  # [100, 200], dtype Int64

# Same dtype, same data — these all upcast correctly:
s.sum()                        # 200
s.prod()                       # 10000
s.groupby([0, 0]).cumsum()     # [100, 200], dtype int64[pyarrow]
```

### Issue Description

I ran into this using int8 for the target variable in a parquet-backed training run. A cumulative bad count over a score-sorted target is how you build a gains or KS table, and with a 0/1 target the running total exceeds int8 on the 128th positive row.

`cumsum` on an integer ArrowDtype raises instead of widening the accumulator, so any series whose running total exceeds the storage width fails. Three rows of value 50 in an `int8[pyarrow]` column is enough to trigger it.
 
Every integer width is affected at its own boundary. The numpy-backed and masked equivalents widen to 64-bit and return the correct value:

| dtype | value | Arrow | numpy |
|---|---|---|---|
| int8 | 127 | ArrowInvalid | [127, 254] |
| int16 | 32767 | ArrowInvalid | [32767, 65534] |
| int32 | 2147483647 | ArrowInvalid | [2147483647, 4294967294] |
| uint8 | 255 | ArrowInvalid | [255, 510] |
| int64 | 2\*\*63-1 | ArrowInvalid | [9223372036854775807, -2] |
 
`cumprod`, `agg("cumsum")` and `Series + Series` fail the same way. `cummax` and `cummin` are unaffected, no overflow is possible.
 
But the same dtype widens correctly everywhere else. So:
 
```python
s = pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]")
s.sum()                       # 200
s.prod()                      # 10000
s.groupby([0, 0]).cumsum()    # [100, 200], int64[pyarrow]
```

So `Series.cumsum` and `SeriesGroupBy.cumsum` disagree on identical input.
 
This is present on 2.3.3 with the same pyarrow, so this is not a 3.0 regression.
 
### Root Cause:
 
`ArrowExtensionArray._accumulate` widens before accumulating, but only for temporal types
(pandas/core/arrays/arrow/array.py):
 
```python
convert_to_int = (
    pa.types.is_temporal(pa_dtype) and name in ["cummax", "cummin"]
) or (pa.types.is_duration(pa_dtype) and name == "cumsum")
 
if convert_to_int:
    if pa_dtype.bit_width == 32:
        data_to_accum = data_to_accum.cast(pa.int32())
    else:
        data_to_accum = data_to_accum.cast(pa.int64())
 
try:
    result = pyarrow_meth(data_to_accum, skip_nulls=skipna, **kwargs)
except pa.ArrowNotImplementedError as err:
    msg = f"operation '{name}' not supported for dtype '{self.dtype}'"
    raise TypeError(msg) from err
```
 
Integer types skip the cast and go into `cumulative_sum_checked` at their native width. The existing `except` translates `ArrowNotImplementedError` into a TypeError but does not cover `ArrowInvalid`, so the pyarrow error surfaces raw with no column or dtype context. `_reduce` already applies the upcast rule, which is why `.sum()` works on the same data.
 

### Expected Behavior

```python
pd.Series([100, 100], dtype="int8[pyarrow]").cumsum()
# [100, 200], dtype int64[pyarrow]
```
 
Widen narrow integer types to `int64`/`uint64` before accumulating, matching `_reduce` and the other two backends.
 
Behavior at the 64-bit boundary is a different question. numpy and masked wrap silently there (`[2**63-1, -2]`), so raising is defensible and I am not asking for it to change. The narrow widths are the part that looks unintended.

comments.body:
I dug into this and the root cause is a unit-inference mismatch between the writer and reader, not corruption of the timestamps themselves.

On write, to_json defaults to date_format="epoch" with date_unit="ms", so datetimes are serialized as epoch milliseconds (e.g. 2015-01-01 → 1420070400000).

On read, read_json doesn't know the unit — date_unit defaults to None, so Parser._try_convert_to_date guesses by trying ("s", "ms", "us", "ns") in order and taking the first that fits within nanosecond bounds. Because this is greedy and order-dependent, the chosen unit depends on the magnitude of the values: large ms timestamps happen to skip "s" (out-of-bounds) and land on "ms", but smaller values can be accepted as "s" first, which is what plants everything near 1970.

So the same file round-trips differently depending on the timestamp values, which is why this is so confusing — passing date_unit="ms" (matching the writer's default) fixes it, as does the reporter's manual to_datetime(..., unit="ms").

A couple of questions before anyone picks this up, since the epoch default is itself deprecated (Pandas4Warning) in favor of ISO:

Is the intended long-term answer here just to steer users to orient="table" / ISO for lossless round-trips, making this a docs/deprecation matter rather than a bug fix?
Or is there appetite for making the epoch read path less surprising in the interim — e.g. preferring the writer's default date_unit on read, or warning when unit inference is ambiguous?

Happy to put up a PR in whichever direction the team prefers.

Columns that do match the name heuristic are where the unit-mismatch can actually produce wrong dates.

Agreed this is really a documentation matter rather than a code bug: to_json defaults to date_format="epoch" with date_unit="ms", while read_json infers the unit independently, so the two defaults can disagree and lose information unless date_format/date_unit are set consistently on both sides. (Worth noting the epoch default is already deprecated in favor of ISO, which would eventually remove the mismatch.)

Would a short note in the read_json/to_json docs — flagging that the epoch round-trip is lossy across mismatched units and recommending orient="table" or matched date_unit — be welcome? Happy to put that up if so.

issues.title: BUG: read_csv fails to finalize index when engine='pyarrow' and dtype is scalar (or dict without an index specified)
issues.body:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python from io import StringIO test=""" col1,col2 10,1 20,2 """ f=StringIO(test) import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa # For AttributeError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype='int64[pyarrow]', dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) # For IndexError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype={'col2': 'int64[pyarrow]'}, dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) print(df.info()) # Simplified example here; see below for more complete testing results ``` ### Issue Description Using `read_csv` raises an `AttributeError` if... - `index_col` is specified, and - `engine='pyarrow'` is specified, and - `dtype` is specified as a scalar or a `dict` that doesn't include the index column ### Scenario A: Scalar dtype raises AttributeError The AttributeError occurs in `ArrowParserWrapper._finalize_index` ([3.0.5](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L202) | [main](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/795cd84559d9147679bfe8461853569727a5ee69/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L390)) when it tries to call `self.dtype.get(item)` on a scalar dtype (e.g., 'int64[pyarrow]' or pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())) instead of a dictionary.
Simplified traceback of AttributeError ``` File "deleteme.py", line 10, in df = pd.read_csv( f, ...<3 lines>... index_col='col1', # Works fine if removed ) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 202, in _finalize_index if self.dtype.get(item) is not None ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get' ```
### Scenario B: Dictionary dtype missing the index column raises IndexError If a dictionary is passed to `dtype` but the index column is omitted from the keys, it looks like the wrapper engine incorrectly handles the remaining columns during `_finalize_dtype`, leading to an `IndexError` down the line.
Simplified traceback of IndexError ``` File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 203, in _finalize_index else (frame.columns[item], self.dtype.get(frame.columns[item])) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\indexes\base.py", line 5425, in __getitem__ result = getitem(key) File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\arrow\array.py", line 780, in __getitem__ raise IndexError( ...<2 lines>... ) IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices ```
## Reproducible testing code I tested several different combinations of `dtype`, `engine`, and `index_col` in a local environment and in Google Colab. The results are summarized below.
```python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa f = 'deleteme.csv' pd.DataFrame({'col1':[10, 20], 'col2':[1, 2]}).to_csv(f, index=False) pd_arrow_int64 = pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64()) # Any of the following dtype specifications have the same test results py_int64 = pd_arrow_int64 py_int64 = 'int64[pyarrow]' py_int64 = {'col1': pd_arrow_int64, 'col2': pd_arrow_int64} def works_as_expected_no_index(py_int64): """Can specify what you want if index_col is omitted""" # Specify dtype df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64) df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, engine='pyarrow') df3 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') # No dtype; infer with dtype_backend, with or without engine df4 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype_backend='pyarrow') df5 = pd.read_csv(f, engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df2) and df2.equals(df3) assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.equals(df4) and df4.equals(df5) def works_as_expected_with_index_no_engine(py_int64): """Can specify dtype or engine, but not both, unless dtype is a dict""" # Omit engine; specify dtype df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1') df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df2) assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.index.dtype == pd_arrow_int64 # Omit dtype; specify engine df3 = pd.read_csv(f, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.equals(df3) def raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine(py_int64): try: df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=py_int64, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') except AttributeError as e: print(f"AttributeError: {e}") #################################### # AttributeError related #################################### works_as_expected_no_index(py_int64) works_as_expected_with_index_no_engine(py_int64) # Raises ➡️ 'ArrowDtype' object has no attribute 'get' raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine(pd_arrow_int64) # Raises ➡️ 'str' object has no attribute 'get' raises_error_with_index_and_both_dtype_and_engine('int64[pyarrow]') #################################### # IndexError related #################################### # Mostly works as expected if dtype is a dict, but it triggers if index dtype not specfied def works_with_engine_if_dtype_specified_for_index(py_int64): """Works if specifying the dtype for the index using a dict. Other column detype is optional""" dd = {'col1':pd_arrow_int64, 'col2':pd_arrow_int64} df1 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') dd = {'col1':pd_arrow_int64} df2 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') assert df1.dtypes.eq(pd_arrow_int64).all() assert df1.index.dtype == pd_arrow_int64 assert df1.equals(df2) try: dd = {'col2': pd_arrow_int64} df3 = pd.read_csv(f, dtype=dd, index_col='col1', engine='pyarrow', dtype_backend='pyarrow') except IndexError as e: print(f"IndexError: {e}") # Raises ➡️ only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices works_with_engine_if_dtype_specified_for_index(pd_arrow_int64) ```

issues.title: BUG: Undocumented, Inconsistent matplotlib figure usage (Series.hist vs Series.plot.hist)
issues.body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

**Note**: Please read [this guide](https://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports) detailing how to provide the necessary information for us to reproduce your bug.

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
# Your code here
from pandas import DataFrame
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

d = DataFrame({'y1':[0,1,2,3], 'y2':[3,4,5,6]}, index=[0,1,2,3])

# A new matplotlib figure is created
print(plt.gcf().number)
d.hist()
print(plt.gcf().number)  # new figure is created, current matplotlib figure is the new one

# Can NOT assign a figure to a dataframe plot
figure = plt.figure()
print(figure.number)
print(plt.gcf().number)
d.hist(figure=figure)  # Throws an exception
print(plt.gcf().number)  # new figure is still created! current matplotlib figure is the new one

# Can assign a figure to a Series histogram
figure1 = plt.figure()
figure2 = plt.figure()  # Current figure is always the last one created
print(figure1.number)
print(figure2.number)
print(plt.gcf().number)
d['y1'].hist(figure=figure1)
print(plt.gcf().number)  # Current figure stays the same
figure1.show() # This works

# Can NOT assign a figure to a Series histogram when using the .plot CachedAccessor
# However, it does not create a new figure
figure1 = plt.figure()
figure2 = plt.figure()  # Current figure is always the last one created
print(figure1.number)
print(figure2.number)
print(plt.gcf().number)
d['y1'].plot.hist(figure=figure1)  # Throws an exception!
print(plt.gcf().number)  # Current figure stays the same
```

#### Problem description

It is currently impossible to assign a plot of a DataFrame to an existing figure.  The functionality is just broken.

The API to set a Series to an existing figure is almost completely broken (with the exception of the direct hist function).
There is a workaround in setting the global current figure `plt.figure(old_figure.number)`, but that does not work if `plt.Figure()` is used.

#### Expected Output

All three examples accept the `figure=` argument, and use it.

I have examined the issue further.

It looks like Series.hist is using [hist_series](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/de5349a4820fd35aeac35ef2538eb564e0e11292/pandas/plotting/_core.py#L18) directly, which bypasses all the logic which is causing the problem.

The issue with DataFrame vs Series is that series plots always set [`reuse_plot=True`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/de5349a4820fd35aeac35ef2538eb564e0e11292/pandas/plotting/_core.py#L896).  I have confirmed that that option allows the work around to work for DataFrame plots as well.  Though why Series plots get special treatment is a mystery.  I suggest removing that special behavior, or at least documenting the default as different and allowing someone to manually set it to False.

The main problem is the matplotlib back-end [plot function](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/de5349a4820fd35aeac35ef2538eb564e0e11292/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/__init__.py#L54) only handles "reuse_plot", and can't handle the "figure" argument.

```python
index = pd.date_range('1/1/2000', periods=9, freq='6H')
series = pd.Series([2, 3, 6, 9, 5, 1, 3, 9, 4], index=index)

series

Freq: 6H, dtype: int64
```
#### Problem description
This has been asked about in a stackoverflow question, but the answer is inefficient and only works for regular time series.
If we have a time series where each value is a discrete measurement, resampling/aggregating would require some kind of interpolation assumption across the resampling period. In it's simplest form, a linear interpolation would just require the time series to be shifted back one step (using the shift(-1)) and take the pandas resampled mean of the original and shifted time series.

#### Expected Output
```python
index = pd.date_range('1/1/2000', periods=9, freq='6H')
series = pd.Series([2, 3, 6, 9, 5, 1, 3, 9, 4], index=index)
series_new = (series + series.shift(-1))/2
res_good = series_new.resample('D').mean()

res_good
2000-01-01    5.375
2000-01-02    4.375
2000-01-03      NaN
```
Compared to the below which only utilizes the values within the resampling period as if the values represented some kind of aggregate measurement since the last time stamp...
```python
res_bad1 = series.resample('D').mean()
2000-01-01    5.0
2000-01-02    4.5
2000-01-03    4.0
```
If there was a closed=both option...
```python
2000-01-01    5.0
2000-01-02    4.0
```

Thanks for the reply. Could you please run through my example in my original post?

The resample method in Pandas inherently assumes that the input data is an aggregate value from the last timestamp to the current timestamp as resample is a simple grouping of timestamp indexes. When data represents instantaneous/discrete values at a particular time, this simple grouping of time indexes for resampling is insufficient as there must be an interpolation assumption to fill in all the times between the instantaneous values. In it's simplest form, a linear interpolation between the points would then represent the mean value over that time period, which then could be fed to the resample method.

issues.title: BUG: use of partition_cols raises incompatibility between fastparquet & pyarrow
issues.body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
import pandas as pd
import fastparquet as fp
from os import path as os_path

df = pd.DataFrame({'ab': [1, 2, 3], 'a':['a', 'b', 'c']})
file = os_path.expanduser('~/Documents/code/data/test.parquet')

# Case 1: write: pandas/pyarrow      || read: pandas/pyarrow
# OK    : 'ab' column is read back with type 'category'
# NOOK  : does not naturally overwrite (file names are different)
#         as a consequence, df that is read back contains twice more data.
# OK    : with snappy not installed, naturally does not compress data.
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'])
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'])
df_rec_pd1 = pd.read_parquet(file)
print(df_rec_pd1['ab'])

# Case 2: write: pandas/fastparquet  || read: pandas/fastparquet
# OK    : 'ab' column is read back with type 'category'
# OK    : naturally overwrites (same file names)
# NOOK  : with snappy not installed, it does not naturally not compress the data,
#         and use of 'compression' keyword is required to specify 'uncompressed'.
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'], engine='fastparquet', compression='uncompressed')
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'], engine='fastparquet', compression='uncompressed')
df_rec_pd2 = pd.read_parquet(file, engine='fastparquet')
print(df_rec_pd2['ab'])

# Case 3: write: pandas/fastparquet  || read: pandas/pyarrow
# OK    : 'ab' column is read back with type 'category'
# OK    : naturally overwrites (same file names)
# NOOK  : with snappy not installed, it does not naturally not compress the data,
#         and use of 'compression' keyword is required to specify 'uncompressed'.
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'], engine='fastparquet', compression='uncompressed')
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'], engine='fastparquet', compression='uncompressed')
df_rec_pd3 = pd.read_parquet(file)
print(df_rec_pd3['ab'])

# Case 4: write: pandas/pyarrow      || read: pandas/fastparquet
# NOOK  : reading does not work. pyarrow does not generate common metada which
#         fastparquet is looking for.
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'])
df.to_parquet(file, partition_cols=['ab'])
df_rec_pd4 = pd.read_parquet(file, engine='fastparquet')
print(df_rec_pd4['ab'])

# Case 5: write: fastparquet         || read: pandas/pyarrow
# OK    : 'ab' column is read back with type 'category'
# OK    : naturally overwrites (same file names)
fp.write(file, df, file_scheme='hive', partition_on=['ab'], compression='BROTLI')
fp.write(file, df, file_scheme='hive', partition_on=['ab'], compression='BROTLI')
df_rec_fp_pd = pd.read_parquet(file)

# Case 6: write: fastparquet         || read: fastparquet
# OK    : nothing to say, perfect :)
fp.write(file, df, file_scheme='hive', partition_on=['ab'])
fp.write(file, df, file_scheme='hive', partition_on=['ab'])
df_rec_fp = fp.ParquetFile(file).to_pandas()

# Case 7: write: pandas/pyarrow      || read: fastparquet
# NOOK  : reading does not work. It seems that even if snappy is not available
#         at writing, it is indicated in metadata as the engine that has been
#         used. As fastparquet is not finding it, it raise an error.
df.to_parquet(file)
df_rec_pd_fp = fp.ParquetFile(file).to_pandas()

# Case 8: write: pandas/pyarrow      || read: fastparquet
# NOOK  : bug already reported: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/39480
#         It seems pandas/pyarrow is not writing categories of int as categories.
df.to_parquet(file, compression='BROTLI')
df_rec_pd_fp = fp.ParquetFile(file).to_pandas()
```

#### Problem description

Hi. I report here 4 different problems as far as I can see (a 5th related one having been reported earlier in [#39480](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/39480)). Trying to synthetize:

- when using `partition_cols` in `to_parquet`, the ways it is managed by fastparquet and pyarrow are different. Most notably, fastparquet is writing common metdata in the root directory, while pyarrow ...? I don't know what it does, but at least, it does not write this 'common metadata' file. This raises a bug as in case 4: writing with pyarrow, reading with fastparquet. fastparquet does not find the common metadata file and refuses to read the data
  
- when not having 'snappy' installed, for writing step, no error is raised with pyarrow. But when read back with fastparquet, this time, reader believes it has been compressed with 'snappy' and complains not to find it. This raises the error as in case 7.

- when not having 'snappy' installed, for the writing and reading steps, could the writer and reader simply/naturally fall back to 'uncompressed'? With fastparquet, this forces the user to add the parameter `compression` set to `uncompressed` as in cases  2, & 3.

- when using `partition_cols` with pyarrow, names of parquet files are always different. Hence, writing twice the same dataset will result in duplicating the data (on the opposite, fastparquet uses always the same file names, which ensures natural overwriting), as in case 1.

comments.body:
OK, there are a few things here.

- the default compression in fastparquet is in fact none. When called from pandas, though, it's snappy (because they wanted to choose one of the two defaults to go with), causing the problem. I don't believe arrow uses python-snappy, so that can compress without it. Note that the newest fastparquet now has a hard dependency on cramjam, which includes snappy, so it will always be available.
- indeed pyarrow does not write the metadata by default, but I believe it can. Fastparquet always does. As of the latest release, fastparquet can be passed a directory and it will find the data files just as pyarrow does. Previously, you had to use glob and pass a list of data files.
- in dask we has a lot of discussion about overwriting. It seems the best to explicitly delete the contents of a directory before writing to it, unless "append" is specified. Dask now allows for a filename template (perhaps still in PR) to specify the names of the data flies; but this is not done in the backend libraries themselves. There's probably no pressing need for pandas to implement this.
